topic: Navigation internals: back stack, NavController & Compose

questions.question: Why does calling viewModel() inside a NavHost destination give a ViewModel scoped to that destination?
options: NavHost creates a new Activity for each destination
viewModel() reads the route string and caches by it in a global map
The ViewModel is scoped to the NavController, shared by all destinations
Each NavBackStackEntry is a ViewModelStoreOwner provided to its content
questions.explanation: Each NavBackStackEntry is a LifecycleOwner, ViewModelStoreOwner and SavedStateRegistryOwner, and NavHost provides it as the local owner for that destination's content. So ViewModels live as long as the entry is on the back stack. A single Activity hosts all destinations.

questions.question: A ViewModel scoped to a destination's NavBackStackEntry is cleared as soon as you navigate forward to another destination.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Navigating forward keeps the previous entry on the back stack, so its ViewModelStore stays alive and the ViewModel is reused when you come back. It is cleared when the entry is popped off (and not saved with saveState).

questions.question: In a Compose NavHost you navigate from A to B and the transition finishes. What is A's NavBackStackEntry lifecycle state?
options: DESTROYED
STARTED
RESUMED
CREATED
questions.explanation: Entries that are on the back stack but not visible are moved to CREATED: still alive with their ViewModels and saved state, but not started. Only the visible top entry reaches RESUMED. DESTROYED happens when the entry is popped.

questions.question: In bottom-navigation code, what does `popUpTo(startDestination) { saveState = true }` combined with `restoreState = true` achieve?
options: Popped entries are destroyed, but their route strings are logged for analytics
Popped entries' ViewModels and saved state are kept for restoring the tab
The whole back stack is written to disk so it survives the user clearing the app
Each tab gets its own NavController, created on demand and kept in memory
questions.explanation: saveState keeps the state of the entries being popped (their ViewModels and saved instance state) instead of clearing it, and restoreState brings that saved stack back on the next navigate to the tab. This is how multiple back stacks work with a single NavController.

questions.question: Which statements about type-safe navigation in Navigation 2.8+ are true? Select all that apply.
options: Routes are defined as @Serializable classes or objects
Arguments can be read with toRoute<T>() on a NavBackStackEntry or SavedStateHandle
Route classes must implement Parcelable to be used with navigate()
Custom argument types need a NavType supplied through typeMap
Arguments are held only in memory and are lost on process death
questions.explanation: Navigation 2.8 uses kotlinx.serialization to turn route objects into destinations and arguments; toRoute rebuilds the object. Primitive-like types work out of the box, custom types need a NavType. Arguments are stored in the entry's saved state, so they survive process death, and Parcelable isn't required.

questions.question: The app is killed in the background while three destinations are on the back stack. When the user returns, what does Navigation restore?
options: Nothing; the NavHost restarts at the start destination
The back stack, arguments and SavedStateHandle data, with new ViewModels
Only the top destination, without the entries below it
The back stack, along with the original ViewModel instances from before
questions.explanation: NavController saves its back stack into the host's saved state, including each entry's arguments and saved state. On restore it rebuilds the entries, and ViewModels are recreated fresh but can read their SavedStateHandle. In-memory ViewModel instances can't survive the process dying.

questions.question: In Navigation 3, the back stack is a list of keys that your code owns and changes directly (for example adding and removing entries), rather than state hidden inside a NavController.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Navigation 3 hands the back stack to you as observable state, typically a snapshot state list of keys, and a display composable renders it. Navigating is just adding or removing items. This is a major break from Navigation 2's NavController-owned back stack.

questions.question: Screens in a nested checkout graph share a ViewModel from `viewModel(navController.getBackStackEntry<CheckoutGraph>())`. When is it cleared?
options: When the user leaves the first screen of the graph
When the Activity goes to the background
When the nested graph's own entry is popped
Never; graph-scoped ViewModels live for the whole lifetime of the process
questions.explanation: A nested graph has its own NavBackStackEntry below its destinations, and that entry is the ViewModelStoreOwner here. The ViewModel stays while any part of the graph is on the back stack and is cleared once the graph entry is popped. Backgrounding the app doesn't clear ViewModelStores.

questions.question: Which statements about NavBackStackEntry lifecycles are true? Select all that apply.
options: An entry's lifecycle never goes above its host's: if the Activity stops, the visible entry stops too
Every entry on the back stack is RESUMED so it can keep updating
A popped entry isn't DESTROYED until its exit transition has finished
Popping an entry without saveState clears its ViewModelStore
An entry's ViewModels are cleared as soon as it drops to CREATED
questions.explanation: Entry lifecycles are capped by the host lifecycle, and Compose Navigation keeps a popped entry alive until its exit animation completes, then destroys it and clears its ViewModels. Hidden entries sit at CREATED with ViewModels intact, and only the visible entry is RESUMED.

questions.question: What does `launchSingleTop = true` do when you navigate to the destination that is already at the top of the back stack?
options: It reuses the top entry instead of pushing a duplicate
It pops the whole back stack and starts the destination again
It throws, because the destination is already displayed
It pushes a copy and then removes the original entry
questions.explanation: Without it, navigating to the current destination pushes a second copy, so the user has to press back twice. With launchSingleTop the existing entry stays on top. It doesn't clear other entries; that's what popUpTo is for.
